concepts: Diploid vs haploid — body (somatic) cells are diploid (2n), with two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent; gametes (sperm and egg) are haploid (n), with one copy. Fertilization restores the diploid number.

Two divisions, one DNA copy — meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, meiosis II separates sister chromatids, like mitosis. DNA is copied only once, so four haploid cells result from one starting cell.
Crossing over — in prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange segments, creating new combinations of alleles on each chromosome. This is the biggest source of new genetic combinations.

Independent assortment — in metaphase I, each homologous pair lines up independently of the others, so the mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes in each gamete is random. With 23 pairs, there are over 8 million possible combinations.

Errors: nondisjunction — when chromosomes fail to separate, a gamete gets an extra chromosome or one too few. Fertilization then produces conditions like Down syndrome (an extra chromosome 21) or Turner syndrome (a missing X).

example.q: Two full siblings share the same parents but look different and have different blood types. Explain how meiosis guarantees this — using crossing over and independent assortment.
steps: First, crossing over: during meiosis in each parent, homologous chromosomes swap segments, so the chromosomes a parent passes on are new mixtures of their own parents' DNA — never the same mix twice.

Second, independent assortment: each of the 23 chromosome pairs lines up randomly in metaphase I, so each gamete gets a random combination of maternal and paternal chromosomes — over 8 million possibilities per parent.
Third, fertilization: the two random gametes combine, multiplying the possibilities — the chance of two siblings receiving the same combination is astronomically small.
Conclusion: meiosis is a shuffling machine. Mitosis preserves the genome; meiosis reshuffles it, which is why sexual reproduction produces variety and why evolution has raw material to work with.

practice.q: Why does meiosis involve two divisions but only one round of DNA replication?
practice.a: Because the goal is to halve the chromosome number: one replication doubles the DNA, and two divisions split it twice, leaving each of the four gametes with a single haploid set.

practice.q: A child is born with Down syndrome (three copies of chromosome 21). At what stage did the error most likely occur, and what is the error called?
practice.a: Nondisjunction — most likely in meiosis I or II in one parent, when the two copies of chromosome 21 failed to separate, so a gamete carried two copies and the fertilized egg ended up with three.

lessons.takeaway: Meiosis halves the chromosome number in two divisions and shuffles the genome by crossing over and independent assortment — so every gamete is unique, and every child is a new combination.

lessons.title: Mendel and the Patterns of Inheritance
lessons.intro: In the 1860s, Gregor Mendel grew thousands of pea plants and counted what he saw — and in doing so, he discovered the rules of inheritance a century before DNA was understood. Traits are passed as discrete units (genes), each organism carries two copies (alleles), and the copies separate when gametes form. Mendel's ratios — 3:1, 9:3:3:1 — are the predictable outcomes of those rules, and they still explain how traits run in families today.
concepts: Genes and alleles — a gene is a DNA segment for a trait; alleles are its versions (for example, purple vs white flower). An organism carries two alleles, one from each parent.

Dominant and recessive — a dominant allele masks a recessive one in a heterozygote (one of each). The recessive trait appears only in a homozygote with two recessive alleles. Dominant does not mean common — it means expressed.
Genotype vs phenotype — the genotype is the alleles an organism carries (e.g., Pp); the phenotype is the trait you see (purple flowers). Different genotypes can produce the same phenotype.

Mendel's laws — the law of segregation: the two alleles separate when gametes form, so each gamete carries one. The law of independent assortment: alleles for different genes sort independently (for genes on different chromosomes).

Punnett squares and probability — a Punnett square maps the possible gamete combinations and their probabilities: a cross of two heterozygotes (Pp × Pp) gives a 3:1 phenotypic ratio; a dihybrid cross (PpYy × PpYy) gives 9:3:3:1.

example.q: Two parents with brown eyes have a child with blue eyes. The parents insist the child must not be theirs. Using Mendel's rules, explain why blue-eyed children of brown-eyed parents are not only possible but expected sometimes.
steps: First, set up the genetics: brown eyes are dominant (B) over blue (b), so the parents are brown-eyed but each must carry a hidden blue allele — both are heterozygotes (Bb).
Second, work the cross: each parent passes B half the time and b half the time, so the Punnett square gives BB, Bb, Bb, and bb — a 3:1 ratio of brown to blue.
Third, read the result: one child in four, on average, inherits b from both parents and has blue eyes — the recessive allele was there all along, masked in the parents.

Conclusion: the parents' claim fails the genetics — a blue-eyed child is the expected outcome in a quarter of their children, and the recessive allele's invisibility in a heterozygote is exactly what Mendel discovered.

practice.q: A pea plant with genotype Tt (tall) is crossed with one that is tt (short). What fraction of the offspring will be short, and what is their genotype?
practice.a: Half the offspring will be short. The Tt parent gives T or t equally, the tt parent gives only t, so the offspring are Tt (tall) or tt (short) in equal proportions — the tt ones are short.

practice.q: Why is 'dominant' not the same as 'most common'? Give an example.
practice.a: Dominant only means the allele is expressed when present; frequency depends on the population. Huntington's disease is caused by a dominant allele, yet it is rare — dominance does not make an allele spread.

lessons.takeaway: Mendel's rules — two alleles per gene, segregation into gametes, dominant masking recessive — turn inheritance into predictable ratios: 3:1 for one trait, 9:3:3:1 for two.

BIO101.mastery_rubric: Explain cell structure and energy flow, trace information from DNA to protein, and predict simple inheritance patterns. Final grade 70% or higher.

lessons.title: Chemistry and the Scientific Method
lessons.intro: Chemistry is the study of matter — what it is made of, how it changes, and why. Every medicine, battery, loaf of bread, and breath of air is chemistry in action. But chemistry is not a list of facts to memorize; it is a science, which means its claims are earned by the scientific method: observe, hypothesize, test, and revise. This lesson sets up the whole course: what chemists study, and how they know what they claim to know.
concepts: Matter and its properties — matter is anything with mass that takes up space. Physical properties (colour, density, melting point) can be observed without changing what a substance is; chemical properties (flammability, reactivity with acid) describe how it changes into something else.

Observation and hypothesis — science starts with a careful observation and a question, then a hypothesis: a testable, falsifiable explanation. 'Salt makes water boil faster because it raises the boiling point' can be tested; 'salt makes water boil faster because it wants to' cannot.

Experiment and variables — the independent variable is what the experimenter changes; the dependent variable is what is measured; controlled variables are kept the same. A control group gives a baseline for comparison.

Theory and law — a scientific law describes a pattern (the law of conservation of mass: mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction). A theory explains why the pattern holds (atomic theory). A theory is not a guess — it is a well-tested explanation.
Measurement and the SI system — chemists measure in SI units: metres, kilograms, seconds, kelvin, and moles. A measurement is only useful with its unit and a sense of its uncertainty.

example.q: A student notices that sugar dissolves faster in hot tea than in iced tea. Design a proper experiment to test whether temperature causes the difference.
steps: First, state a hypothesis: 'Sugar dissolves faster in water at higher temperatures.' It is specific, testable, and falsifiable — a result showing no difference would prove it wrong.

Second, set up controlled trials: identical glasses, the same amount of water, the same mass of sugar, stirred the same number of times — differing only in the independent variable, water temperature (for example 5 °C, 25 °C, 50 °C, 80 °C).
Third, measure the dependent variable the same way each time: the time until no solid sugar is visible. Repeat each temperature three times and average, so one odd result cannot decide the outcome.

Conclusion: if dissolving time falls steadily as temperature rises, the data support the hypothesis; if the times are the same, the hypothesis is rejected and something else — stirring, perhaps — must explain the original observation.

practice.q: A company claims its new cleaning spray kills 99.9% of germs, based on one test in one kitchen. What is wrong with this evidence?
practice.a: There is no control group (a kitchen cleaned with plain water), no replication, and no stated method — one test cannot separate the spray's effect from the wiping, the kitchen, or chance. A good experiment needs a control, repeats, and identical conditions except the product being tested.

practice.q: Is the melting point of ice a physical or a chemical property? How do you know?
practice.a: Physical — ice melting into liquid water changes its state, not its identity: the substance is still H2O. A chemical property would involve ice changing into a different substance, as in reacting with something.

lessons.takeaway: Chemistry studies matter and its changes, and its claims are earned by the scientific method: a testable hypothesis, controlled experiments with one variable changed at a time, and results that can be replicated — laws describe the patterns, theories explain them.

lessons.title: Units, Significant Figures and Dimensional Analysis
lessons.intro: A number without a unit is a rumour. '5' could mean 5 grams, 5 litres, or 5 metres — and the difference between 5 grams and 5 kilograms of a chemical can be the difference between a safe experiment and a dangerous one. Chemists convert between units constantly, and they track significant figures so a result never claims more precision than the measurements behind it. Dimensional analysis — the factor-label method — is the single most useful calculation skill in this course.
concepts: SI base units and prefixes — length (metre), mass (kilogram), time (second), temperature (kelvin), amount (mole). Prefixes scale by powers of ten: milli- (10^-3), centi- (10^-2), kilo- (10^3), mega- (10^6). A millilitre is one-thousandth of a litre.

Significant figures — the digits in a measurement that carry real information. All non-zero digits count; zeros between digits count; trailing zeros after a decimal count; leading zeros never count. 0.00450 has three significant figures; 100.0 has four.

Exact vs measured numbers — counted numbers and defined conversions (12 inches = 1 foot exactly) have unlimited significant figures. Measured numbers are limited by the instrument: a balance reading 2.54 g is not 2.5400 g.

Rounding rules for calculations — in multiplication and division, the answer has as many significant figures as the least precise input. In addition and subtraction, the answer is limited by the least precise decimal place.

Dimensional analysis — multiply by conversion factors written as fractions equal to 1 (e.g. 1000 m / 1 km), arranging them so unwanted units cancel and only the wanted unit remains. The units themselves check the work.

example.q: A lab procedure calls for 250 mL of solution, but the only measuring cylinder is marked in litres and the balance reads in grams. The solution's density is 1.05 g/mL. How many grams of solution is 250 mL, and how many litres is it? Give answers to the correct significant figures.
steps: First, convert volume: 250 mL × (1 L / 1000 mL) = 0.250 L. The mL units cancel, leaving litres. 250 has three significant figures, so 0.250 L is right.
Second, find the mass with density as a conversion factor: 250 mL × (1.05 g / 1 mL) = 262.5 g. The mL cancel, leaving grams.

Third, fix the significant figures: 1.05 has three significant figures and 250 has three, so the answer is limited to three: 262.5 g rounds to 263 g (262.5 rounds to 263, since the digit after 2 is 5 followed by nothing — round-half-up here gives 263).
Conclusion: 250 mL is 0.250 L and has a mass of 263 g. Notice how the units cancelled at every step — if a unit had survived that should not be there, the setup was wrong.

practice.q: Convert 3.20 km to metres, and state the answer with the correct number of significant figures.
practice.a: 3.20 km × (1000 m / 1 km) = 3200 m. But 3.20 has three significant figures, so the answer must be written 3.20 × 10^3 m — plain '3200 m' is ambiguous about whether the trailing zeros are significant.

practice.q: A student multiplies 2.5 cm × 4.13 cm and reports 10.325 cm². What is wrong, and what should the answer be?
practice.a: The result claims five significant figures, but 2.5 has only two — the answer can have at most two: 10 cm². Reporting 10.325 cm² pretends the measurement was far more precise than it was.

lessons.takeaway: Every measurement needs a unit and an honest number of significant figures, and dimensional analysis — cancelling units through conversion factors — both converts quantities and checks that the calculation itself is set up correctly.

lessons.title: Atoms, Elements and the Periodic Table
lessons.intro: Everything you can touch is built from about 118 elements, and every element is built from atoms. An atom is mostly empty space: a tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons. The periodic table is the map of this world — it organizes the elements so that elements in the same column behave alike, letting chemists predict the properties of an element they have never seen.
concepts: Subatomic particles — protons (+1 charge, mass ~1 amu) and neutrons (no charge, mass ~1 amu) live in the nucleus; electrons (-1 charge, mass ~1/1836 amu) occupy the space around it. The atom's mass comes almost entirely from the nucleus; its size comes from the electrons.

Atomic number and mass number — the atomic number Z is the number of protons and defines the element (all carbon atoms have Z = 6). The mass number A is protons + neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons.

Isotopes — atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons: carbon-12 (6 neutrons) and carbon-14 (8 neutrons) are both carbon, but carbon-14 is radioactive. Atomic mass on the table is a weighted average of the isotopes.
Ions — atoms that gain or lose electrons become charged: cations are positive (Na+ lost one electron), anions are negative (Cl- gained one). The charge is written as a superscript.

The periodic table — rows (periods) run left to right; columns (groups) run top to bottom. Group 1 (alkali metals) are reactive soft metals; Group 17 (halogens) are reactive nonmetals; Group 18 (noble gases) barely react at all. Metals sit on the left, nonmetals on the right, metalloids along the stair-step line.

example.q: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons, and 17 electrons. Identify the element, its mass number, and whether it is an atom or an ion. Then predict how it is likely to behave chemically.
steps: First, the element: 17 protons means Z = 17, which is chlorine (Cl) on the periodic table.
Second, the mass number: A = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35, so this is chlorine-35, the most common isotope of chlorine.
Third, the charge: 17 protons (+) and 17 electrons (-) balance exactly, so the particle is a neutral atom, not an ion.

Conclusion: chlorine sits in Group 17, the halogens — one electron short of a full outer shell — so it is highly reactive and tends to gain one electron to become Cl-, the chloride ion found in table salt.

practice.q: How many protons, neutrons, and electrons are in a neutral atom of iron-56 (Fe, Z = 26)?
practice.a: Protons = Z = 26; electrons = 26 (neutral atom); neutrons = A − Z = 56 − 26 = 30.

practice.q: Why is the atomic mass of chlorine listed as 35.45 rather than a whole number?
practice.a: Because natural chlorine is a mixture of isotopes — about 76% chlorine-35 and 24% chlorine-37 — and the table's atomic mass is the weighted average of those isotopes, not the mass of any single atom.

lessons.takeaway: The proton count defines the element, the neutron count defines the isotope, and the electron count decides the charge — and the periodic table arranges elements so that neighbours in a column share chemical behaviour, making it chemistry's best prediction tool.

lessons.title: Compounds, Mixtures and Naming Basics
lessons.intro: Pure elements are only the start. Most of the matter around you is compounds — two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio — or mixtures, where substances are just stirred together and keep their own identities. Salt water is a mixture; table salt itself is a compound. Chemists need a naming system so that one name means exactly one substance everywhere in the world, and the rules are simpler than they look.
concepts: Elements vs compounds vs mixtures — an element is one kind of atom; a compound is two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio (water is always H2O); a mixture is a physical blend with variable composition (salt water can be saltier or weaker) whose parts can be separated by physical means.

Homogeneous vs heterogeneous mixtures — homogeneous mixtures (solutions) are uniform throughout, like air or salt water; heterogeneous mixtures are not, like sand in water or a salad, where you can see the separate parts.

Ionic compounds — a metal and a nonmetal transfer electrons: Na+ and Cl- attract into NaCl. The formula is written with the smallest whole-number ratio that makes the total charge zero. Ionic compounds form crystals and conduct electricity when dissolved or melted.

Covalent compounds — two nonmetals share electrons: H2O, CO2, CH4. The formula shows the actual numbers of atoms, and prefixes say how many: mono- (1), di- (2), tri- (3), tetra- (4), penta- (5). CO2 is carbon dioxide.

Naming ionic compounds — name the cation first, then the anion with an -ide ending: MgO is magnesium oxide; CaCl2 is calcium chloride. For metals that form more than one charge (like iron), Roman numerals give the charge: FeCl3 is iron(III) chloride.

example.q: Write the formula for the ionic compound formed from aluminium (Al3+) and oxygen (O2-), and name the covalent compound N2O4.
steps: First, balance the charges for the ionic compound: Al3+ and O2- must combine so the total charge is zero. Two Al3+ give +6; three O2- give -6. So the formula is Al2O3.
Second, check the name: aluminium is the cation, oxygen becomes oxide, so Al2O3 is aluminium oxide — the same compound that makes up sapphires and rubies.
Third, name the covalent compound: N2O4 has two nitrogens and four oxygens, both nonmetals, so use prefixes: di- for two nitrogens, tetra- for four oxygens. The name is dinitrogen tetroxide.
Conclusion: ionic formulas come from charge balance, not prefixes; covalent names come from atom counts. Mixing the two systems up is the most common naming mistake.

practice.q: Is air a compound or a mixture? Explain, and say whether it is homogeneous or heterogeneous.
practice.a: A mixture — air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen physically mixed, not chemically bonded, and its composition varies slightly from place to place. It is homogeneous: the gases are uniformly mixed, so you cannot see separate parts.

practice.q: What is the formula of calcium chloride, and why does it have two chlorines?
practice.a: CaCl2. Calcium forms Ca2+ and chlorine forms Cl-, so two chloride ions are needed to balance the +2 charge of one calcium ion.

lessons.takeaway: Compounds have a fixed composition and are made by chemical bonds; mixtures are physical blends with variable composition. Ionic formulas balance charges to zero, covalent names count atoms with prefixes, and the system gives every substance exactly one name.

lessons.title: The Mole Concept
lessons.intro: Chemists count atoms the way bakers count eggs — by the dozen. But atoms are so tiny that a chemist's 'dozen' has to be enormous: 6.022 × 10^23, Avogadro's number, called one mole. One mole of carbon weighs 12.01 grams; one mole of water weighs 18.02 grams. The mole is the bridge between the invisible world of atoms and the visible world of grams on a balance — and it is the key to every calculation in this course.
concepts: Avogadro's number — 1 mole = 6.022 × 10^23 particles, whether atoms, molecules, or ions. It is the number of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12, and it lets chemists count particles by weighing them.

Molar mass — the mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol, equal to the sum of the atomic masses in its formula. H2O: 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol. The periodic table gives every atomic mass you need.
Moles to grams and back — mass = moles × molar mass; moles = mass ÷ molar mass. These two equations are dimensional analysis with the molar mass as the conversion factor.
Moles to particles — particles = moles × Avogadro's number; moles = particles ÷ Avogadro's number. A mole of anything, from sand grains to stars, contains the same number of items.
Percent composition — the mass percent of each element in a compound: (mass of that element in one mole ÷ molar mass) × 100%. It is how a compound's formula is checked against experiment.

example.q: A chemist has 36.0 g of water. How many moles is that, how many molecules, and what mass of hydrogen does it contain?
steps: First, the molar mass of water: H2O = 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol.
Second, moles: 36.0 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 2.00 mol of water (36.0 has three significant figures, so 2.00 mol).
Third, molecules: 2.00 mol × 6.022 × 10^23 molecules/mol = 1.20 × 10^24 molecules.

Fourth, the hydrogen: each water molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms, so one mole of water contains 2.016 g of hydrogen; 2.00 mol contains 4.03 g. Conclusion: 36.0 g of water is 2.00 mol, about 1.20 × 10^24 molecules, containing 4.03 g of hydrogen.

practice.q: How many grams is 0.500 mol of carbon dioxide, CO2?
practice.a: Molar mass of CO2 = 12.01 + 2(16.00) = 44.01 g/mol. Mass = 0.500 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 22.0 g.

practice.q: A sample contains 3.011 × 10^23 atoms of iron. How many moles is that?
practice.a: Moles = 3.011 × 10^23 ÷ 6.022 × 10^23 = 0.500 mol. (3.011 × 10^23 is exactly half of Avogadro's number, so half a mole.)

lessons.takeaway: One mole is 6.022 × 10^23 particles, and its mass in grams is the molar mass — so weighing a substance is counting its atoms, and the mole connects the atomic scale to the laboratory scale.

lessons.title: Atomic Models and Electron Configuration
lessons.intro: Atoms are too small to see, so our picture of them has been rebuilt again and again: Dalton's solid spheres, Thomson's 'plum pudding', Rutherford's tiny nucleus, Bohr's neat orbits, and today's quantum model, where electrons live in clouds of probability called orbitals. The quantum model is the one that works — and its payoff is electron configuration, the address of every electron in an atom, which predicts how the atom will react.
concepts: The quantum model — electrons occupy orbitals, regions where an electron is likely to be found. Orbitals group into shells (n = 1, 2, 3...) and subshells (s, p, d, f). An s subshell holds 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14.

The Aufbau principle — electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first. The filling order is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d... (the 4s fills before 3d, a quirk that matters for the transition metals).

Pauli exclusion and Hund's rule — no two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers, so each orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins. Hund's rule: within a subshell, electrons spread out into separate orbitals before pairing up.
Writing configurations — carbon (6 electrons): 1s² 2s² 2p². The superscript counts the electrons in that subshell. Noble-gas shorthand shortens it: carbon is [He] 2s² 2p².

Valence electrons — the electrons in the outermost shell, which do the chemistry. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, which is why they behave alike: all Group 1 elements have one valence electron to give away.

example.q: Write the full electron configuration of oxygen (Z = 8) and of iron (Z = 26), and state how many valence electrons each has.
steps: First, oxygen: 8 electrons fill 1s (2), then 2s (2), then 2p (4): 1s² 2s² 2p⁴. Shorthand: [He] 2s² 2p⁴. Its valence shell is n = 2, holding 2 + 4 = 6 valence electrons — so oxygen tends to gain 2 electrons to complete its octet.
Second, iron: 26 electrons fill 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶. Shorthand: [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. Notice 4s fills before 3d.

Third, iron's valence electrons: the outermost shell is n = 4 with 2 electrons, but transition metals also use their d electrons in bonding, so iron commonly loses 2 or 3 electrons (Fe2+ or Fe3+) — the 3d⁶ electrons are chemically active too.
Conclusion: oxygen's 6 valence electrons explain its hunger for 2 more; iron's 4s² 3d⁶ explains its two common charges. Configuration is destiny in chemistry.

practice.q: Write the electron configuration of sodium (Z = 11) and explain, from it, why sodium forms a +1 ion.
practice.a: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ — one electron in its outermost shell. Losing that single 3s electron leaves the stable filled shell of neon, so Na+ is far more stable than neutral Na.

practice.q: Why does Hund's rule say nitrogen (1s² 2s² 2p³) has three unpaired electrons, not one pair and one single?
practice.a: The 2p subshell has three orbitals. Hund's rule puts one electron in each orbital before any pairing, so all three 2p electrons sit alone, unpaired — which makes nitrogen's three unpaired electrons available to form three bonds.

lessons.takeaway: Electrons fill orbitals lowest-energy first, two per orbital with opposite spins, spreading out before pairing — and the resulting configuration, especially the valence electrons, predicts an element's chemistry.

lessons.title: Periodic Trends
lessons.intro: The periodic table is not just a list — it is a landscape with slopes. Atomic size, ionization energy, and electronegativity all change in regular patterns across a period and down a group, and those patterns are explained by two competing forces: the pull of the nucleus and the shielding of inner electrons. Learn the trends and you can rank any set of elements without looking anything up.
concepts: Effective nuclear charge — the net pull an outer electron feels: the nucleus's full positive charge minus the shielding of inner electrons. Across a period, protons are added but shielding barely changes, so the pull grows; down a group, new shells add shielding faster than protons, so the pull weakens.

Atomic radius — across a period, atoms shrink as the growing nuclear pull drags the same shell inward; down a group, atoms grow because each new shell is farther out. Fluorine is small; caesium is huge.

Ionization energy — the energy needed to remove an electron. It rises across a period (electrons are held tighter) and falls down a group (outer electrons are farther and more shielded). Noble gases have the highest ionization energies in their periods.

Electronegativity — an atom's hunger for shared electrons in a bond, on the Pauling scale. It rises across a period and falls down a group; fluorine (4.0) is the most electronegative element, caesium and francium the least.

Exceptions to watch — ionization energy dips at Group 13 (one electron in a new p orbital is easier to remove) and at Group 16 (a paired electron repels its partner). The exceptions prove the orbital model: they happen exactly where the filling pattern predicts.

example.q: Rank Na, Mg, and Al by atomic radius (largest first) and by first ionization energy (highest first). Explain each ranking.
steps: First, locate them: Na, Mg, Al are neighbours in Period 3, Groups 1, 2, 13. Same shell (n = 3), but the nuclear charge grows from 11 to 13 across the row.
Second, atomic radius: across a period, the stronger pull drags the shell inward, so size falls: Na > Mg > Al.

Third, ionization energy: the same growing pull holds electrons tighter, so it costs more energy to remove one: Al > Mg > Na. (Aluminium's value is slightly lower than the simple trend predicts because its outer electron sits in a new 3p orbital, but it still exceeds sodium's.)
Conclusion: across a period, radius falls and ionization energy rises, both driven by effective nuclear charge. Down a group the opposite happens, driven by new shells and shielding.

practice.q: Which is larger: a sodium atom or a sodium ion (Na+)? Why?
practice.a: The sodium atom is larger. Na+ has lost its entire outer shell (the 3s electron), leaving only the smaller n = 2 shell, and its 10 remaining electrons are pulled in by 11 protons — so the cation is much smaller than the atom.

practice.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity in Period 2, and why is it not neon?
practice.a: Fluorine. Electronegativity rises across the period toward the right, but neon, a noble gas, does not form bonds and take shared electrons, so it is assigned no electronegativity value — fluorine, one electron short of a full shell, is the hungriest.

lessons.takeaway: Across a period, atoms shrink and hold electrons tighter as nuclear charge grows; down a group, atoms grow and loosen as new shells shield the pull — and those two forces explain radius, ionization energy, and electronegativity together.

lessons.title: Ionic and Covalent Bonding
lessons.intro: Atoms bond because full outer shells are stable, and bonding is how atoms get there. When the electronegativity difference is large, one atom simply takes the electron — an ionic bond. When the difference is small, the atoms share — a covalent bond. Between the two extremes lies a continuum, and where a bond sits on it decides whether a substance is a salty crystal, a gas, or a diamond.
concepts: The octet rule — atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to reach eight valence electrons (two for hydrogen), matching a noble gas. It is a powerful guide, though not a law: some elements break it.

Ionic bonding — electron transfer between a metal (low electronegativity) and a nonmetal (high). The ions attract into a crystal lattice with high melting points; the solid does not conduct, but the melt or solution does, because the ions can move.
Covalent bonding — electron sharing between two nonmetals. A single bond shares one pair; a double bond two pairs; a triple bond three. Shared pairs are bonding pairs; unshared pairs are lone pairs.

Electronegativity difference and bond type — below ~0.5, nonpolar covalent (electrons shared evenly); 0.5–1.7, polar covalent (shared unevenly); above ~1.7, usually ionic. It is a spectrum, not a wall: even NaCl has a trace of covalent character.

Bond energy and length — stronger bonds are shorter and take more energy to break: triple > double > single. Bond energies explain why some reactions release heat (strong bonds formed) and others absorb it.

example.q: Classify the bonding in HF, NaCl, and Cl2 as ionic, polar covalent, or nonpolar covalent, using electronegativity values (H 2.1, F 4.0, Na 0.9, Cl 3.0).
steps: First, HF: difference = 4.0 − 2.1 = 1.9, which is above the 1.7 line — yet hydrogen fluoride is a polar covalent gas of molecules, not an ionic crystal. The 1.7 line is a guide, not a verdict: fluorine pulls the shared pair strongly toward itself, but the electron is not fully transferred.

Second, NaCl: difference = 3.0 − 0.9 = 2.1, well above the line — ionic. Sodium gives its electron to chlorine; the result is a crystal of Na+ and Cl- ions, high melting point, conducting when melted.
Third, Cl2: difference = 0, two identical atoms — nonpolar covalent, the pair shared exactly evenly.

Conclusion: the difference predicts the trend, but the real test is behaviour — ionic compounds form crystals and conduct when molten; covalent compounds form molecules. HF is the reminder that rules of thumb have exceptions.

practice.q: Why does solid NaCl not conduct electricity, but molten NaCl does?
practice.a: In the solid, the ions are locked in the crystal lattice and cannot move, so no charge can flow. Melted, the lattice breaks and the ions are free to move toward the electrodes, carrying current.

practice.q: Oxygen gas is O2 with a double bond. How many bonding pairs and lone pairs does each oxygen atom have?
practice.a: Each oxygen has 6 valence electrons. Two pairs are shared as the double bond; each oxygen keeps 2 lone pairs (4 electrons). 2 shared pairs + 2 lone pairs = 8 electrons around each oxygen — a full octet.

lessons.takeaway: Ionic bonds transfer electrons between metals and nonmetals into conducting crystal lattices; covalent bonds share electrons between nonmetals into molecules; the electronegativity difference predicts which, but a substance's behaviour is the final judge.

lessons.title: Lewis Structures
lessons.intro: A Lewis structure is a drawing of a molecule's electrons — dots for valence electrons, lines for shared pairs — and it is the single most useful sketch in chemistry. From it you can read the molecule's shape, its polarity, and what reactions it is likely to do. The rules are mechanical: count the valence electrons, connect the atoms, fill the octets, and check the count. Once the rules are automatic, molecules become readable.
concepts: Valence electron count — sum the valence electrons of every atom (and adjust for charge: add one per negative charge, subtract one per positive). This total is the budget; a correct structure uses exactly that many electrons.
The skeleton — the least electronegative atom (never hydrogen) goes in the centre; hydrogens and more electronegative atoms go around it. Connect each pair with a single bond (2 electrons each).

Filling octets — give the outer atoms full octets first (hydrogen gets just 2), then put any leftover electrons on the central atom. If the centre is short, move a lone pair from a neighbour in to make a double or triple bond.

Formal charge — a bookkeeping check: formal charge = valence electrons − (nonbonding electrons + half the bonding electrons). The best structure has formal charges closest to zero, with any negative charge on the most electronegative atom.
Exceptions to the octet — hydrogen (2), boron (often 6), beryllium (4), and elements in Period 3 and below (expanded octets: SF6 has 12 electrons around sulfur) do not always follow the octet rule.

example.q: Draw the Lewis structure of carbon dioxide, CO2.
steps: First, count: carbon has 4 valence electrons, each oxygen 6 — total 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 electrons to place.
Second, the skeleton: carbon is least electronegative, so it goes in the centre with a single bond to each oxygen: O–C–O. That uses 4 electrons, leaving 12.
Third, fill the outer atoms: give each oxygen 6 more electrons (3 lone pairs each), using all 12. Now carbon has only 4 electrons around it — an incomplete octet.

Fourth, fix the centre: move one lone pair from each oxygen in to form double bonds: O=C=O. Now each oxygen has 2 lone pairs + 2 bonds = 8 electrons, carbon has 4 bonds = 8 electrons, and all 16 electrons are used. Formal charges are all zero — this is the correct structure.

practice.q: How many valence electrons are in the nitrate ion, NO3-, and what does the charge do to the count?
practice.a: Nitrogen contributes 5, each oxygen 6 (18 total), and the -1 charge adds 1 more: 24 valence electrons. The extra electron is what makes the ion negative.

practice.q: Why is boron trifluoride, BF3, stable even though boron has only 6 electrons around it?
practice.a: Boron has 3 valence electrons and forms three single bonds to fluorine, giving it 6 shared electrons — an incomplete octet. It is stable because boron is small and the B–F bonds are strong, but the empty orbital makes BF3 eager to accept a lone pair, which is why it is a strong Lewis acid.

lessons.takeaway: A Lewis structure spends exactly the molecule's valence-electron budget: centre atom first, single bonds, outer octets, then multiple bonds to complete the centre — and formal charge picks the best arrangement when more than one is possible.

lessons.title: Molecular Geometry and Polarity (VSEPR)
lessons.intro: A molecule's shape decides what it can do: water is bent, and that bend makes it polar, which makes it a great solvent, which makes life possible. VSEPR theory predicts shape from a simple idea — electron groups repel each other and spread out as far as possible. Count the groups around the central atom, look up the shape, and the molecule's geometry and polarity follow.
concepts: Electron groups — a group is a lone pair, a single bond, a double bond, or a triple bond (a multiple bond counts as one group, because its electrons occupy one region). VSEPR counts groups, not electrons.

The five basic geometries — 2 groups: linear (180°); 3 groups: trigonal planar (120°); 4 groups: tetrahedral (109.5°); 5 groups: trigonal bipyramidal; 6 groups: octahedral (90°). Lone pairs occupy positions too, but the molecule's shape is named by the atoms only.

Lone pairs bend shapes — lone pairs repel more strongly than bonds, squeezing bond angles. CH4 (4 bonds) is tetrahedral; NH3 (3 bonds + 1 lone pair) is trigonal pyramidal; H2O (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs) is bent, with an angle of 104.5°.

Polarity of bonds vs molecules — a polar bond has uneven sharing; a polar molecule has an uneven overall distribution. A molecule with polar bonds can still be nonpolar if its shape is symmetric: CO2's two C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.

Predicting polarity — draw the Lewis structure, find the shape, check each bond's polarity, and add the dipoles as arrows. If they cancel, the molecule is nonpolar; if a net dipole remains, it is polar.

example.q: Predict the shape of ammonia (NH3) and of boron trifluoride (BF3), and decide whether each molecule is polar.
steps: First, ammonia: nitrogen has 5 valence electrons — 3 bonds to hydrogen and 1 lone pair, so 4 electron groups. Four groups arrange tetrahedrally, but with one position taken by a lone pair the atoms form a trigonal pyramid.
Second, ammonia's polarity: each N–H bond is polar (nitrogen pulls harder), and the pyramid shape means the three dipoles do not cancel — they add up along the pyramid's axis. NH3 is polar.

Third, boron trifluoride: boron has 3 bonds and no lone pairs — 3 electron groups, trigonal planar, with 120° angles. Each B–F bond is polar, but the three dipoles point symmetrically outward in a plane.
Conclusion: in BF3 the dipoles cancel exactly, so the molecule is nonpolar despite its polar bonds — shape, not just bond polarity, decides the molecule.

practice.q: Methane (CH4) has four polar C–H bonds (carbon is slightly more electronegative than hydrogen). Is methane polar? Explain.
practice.a: No. CH4 is tetrahedral and perfectly symmetric, so the four small bond dipoles cancel exactly. The molecule has no net dipole — it is nonpolar.

practice.q: Water is bent at 104.5°, not the tetrahedral 109.5°. Why is the angle smaller?
practice.a: Water's oxygen has two lone pairs, which repel more strongly than bonding pairs. They squeeze the two O–H bonds closer together, shrinking the angle from 109.5° to 104.5°.

lessons.takeaway: Electron groups spread out to minimize repulsion, giving five basic geometries; lone pairs bend those shapes, and a molecule is polar only when its bond dipoles fail to cancel — which is why water's bend changes the world.

lessons.title: Balancing Chemical Equations
lessons.intro: A chemical equation is a recipe written in symbols — and like any recipe, it must account for every atom. The law of conservation of mass says atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, only rearranged. Balancing an equation means choosing coefficients so that every element has the same number of atoms on both sides. It is pure bookkeeping, and it is the foundation of every calculation that follows in this course.
concepts: Reactants and products — reactants are written on the left of the arrow, products on the right. The arrow means 'reacts to form'. A balanced equation has equal atoms of each element on both sides.

Coefficients vs subscripts — coefficients (the big numbers in front of a formula) change how many molecules react; subscripts (the small numbers inside a formula) are part of the compound's identity and must NEVER be changed to balance an equation. Change a subscript and you have invented a different substance.

A balancing strategy — balance elements that appear in only one compound on each side first; save pure elements (like O2 or H2) for last; use fractions temporarily if needed, then multiply through to whole numbers.
States of matter — (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. They are labels, not part of the balancing, but they tell you what is really happening in the flask.

Why it matters — a balanced equation is a mole ratio machine: its coefficients say exactly how many moles of each substance react and form. Stoichiometry, the next lessons, runs entirely on these ratios.

example.q: Balance the combustion of propane: C3H8 + O2 → CO2 + H2O.
steps: First, count the unbalanced atoms: left has 3 C and 8 H; right has 1 C and 2 H. Balance carbon first: put a 3 in front of CO2: C3H8 + O2 → 3CO2 + H2O.
Second, balance hydrogen: 8 H on the left need 4 H2O on the right: C3H8 + O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O.
Third, count oxygen on the right: 3CO2 gives 6 O, 4H2O gives 4 O — 10 O atoms total. Oxygen comes as O2, so 5 O2 molecules are needed: C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O.

Conclusion: check every element — C: 3 = 3, H: 8 = 8, O: 10 = 10. The equation is balanced. Notice oxygen, the pure element appearing in only one reactant, was balanced last, exactly as the strategy says.

practice.q: Balance: Fe + O2 → Fe2O3. Why can't you balance it by changing Fe2O3 to Fe2O2?
practice.a: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3. Changing Fe2O3 to Fe2O2 would invent a compound that is not iron(III) oxide — subscripts define the substance, so only coefficients may change.

practice.q: Balance the reaction of aluminium with hydrochloric acid: Al + HCl → AlCl3 + H2.
practice.a: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl3 + 3H2. Check: Al 2 = 2, H 6 = 6, Cl 6 = 6.

lessons.takeaway: A balanced equation obeys conservation of mass: coefficients — never subscripts — are adjusted until every element's atom count matches on both sides, and those coefficients become the mole ratios for all later calculations.

lessons.title: Types of Chemical Reactions
lessons.intro: Thousands of chemical reactions exist, but almost all of them fit into five patterns. Learn to recognize the pattern and you can predict the products of a reaction you have never seen: two things joining, one thing splitting, an element swapping places, two compounds trading partners, or a fuel burning in oxygen. Classification is prediction.
concepts: Combination (synthesis) — A + B → AB. Two or more substances join into one product: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O; CaO + CO2 → CaCO3.
Decomposition — AB → A + B. One compound breaks into two or more pieces, often with heat: 2KClO3 → 2KCl + 3O2; CaCO3 → CaO + CO2.

Single replacement — A + BC → AC + B. A more reactive element displaces a less reactive one: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. The activity series predicts whether the swap happens: an element can only replace one below it.

Double replacement — AB + CD → AD + CB. Two compounds trade partners: AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO3. It happens when one product is a precipitate (solid), a gas, or water — something that leaves the solution.
Combustion — a fuel reacts with oxygen, releasing energy: complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives CO2 + H2O; incomplete combustion (too little oxygen) also makes carbon monoxide or soot.

example.q: Classify each reaction and predict what drives it: (a) 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl; (b) BaCl2 + Na2SO4 → BaSO4 + 2NaCl; (c) Cu + 2AgNO3 → Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag.
steps: First, (a): two elements join into one compound — combination. The driver is the formation of the stable NaCl lattice from reactive sodium and chlorine.
Second, (b): two compounds trade partners — double replacement. The driver is BaSO4, barium sulfate, which is insoluble: it falls out of solution as a white precipitate, pulling the reaction forward.
Third, (c): copper replaces silver — single replacement. The driver is the activity series: copper is more reactive than silver, so it displaces Ag+ from solution, and silver metal appears.
Conclusion: classify by the pattern of atoms, then ask what product leaves the scene — a solid, a gas, water, or a stable lattice — because that is usually what makes the reaction go.

practice.q: A student mixes solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide and a bright yellow solid appears. What type of reaction is this, and what is the solid?
practice.a: Double replacement: Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI → PbI2 + 2KNO3. The yellow solid is lead(II) iodide, PbI2, an insoluble precipitate.

practice.q: Will iron displace copper from copper(II) sulfate solution? Use the activity series: Fe is above Cu.
practice.a: Yes — iron is more reactive than copper, so Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu, and copper metal coats the iron. A metal below copper in the series could not do this.

lessons.takeaway: Most reactions fit five patterns — combination, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement, combustion — and each runs because a product leaves the scene: a precipitate, a gas, water, or a stable compound.

lessons.title: Mole Ratios and Stoichiometric Calculations
lessons.intro: A balanced equation is a recipe in moles, and stoichiometry is cooking by that recipe. If 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen to make 2 moles of water, then any amount scales by the same ratio. With the mole as the unit, you can start from grams of one substance and end at grams — or litres, or molecules — of another. This is the central calculation of chemistry.
concepts: Mole ratios from coefficients — in 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, the ratio H2 : O2 : H2O is 2 : 1 : 2. Any pair of coefficients is a conversion factor between moles of two substances.
The stoichiometry roadmap — grams of A → moles of A (÷ molar mass) → moles of B (× mole ratio) → grams of B (× molar mass). Every problem is this path, sometimes with a shortcut.
Mole ratios are exact — coefficients are counted numbers, so they carry unlimited significant figures and never limit the answer's precision; only the measurements do.
Working with gases — at standard temperature and pressure (STP, 0 °C and 1 atm), one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L. That volume is another conversion factor on the roadmap.
Checking the answer — a mass of product should be the same order of magnitude as the mass of reactant (atoms are conserved). An answer of 500 g from 5 g of reactant means the ratio was flipped.

example.q: How many grams of water form when 8.0 g of hydrogen gas burns in excess oxygen? (2H2 + O2 → 2H2O)
steps: First, moles of hydrogen: molar mass of H2 is 2.016 g/mol, so 8.0 g ÷ 2.016 g/mol = 3.97 mol H2.
Second, the mole ratio: the equation says 2 mol H2 make 2 mol H2O, a ratio of 1:1 — so 3.97 mol H2 make 3.97 mol H2O.
Third, grams of water: 3.97 mol × 18.02 g/mol = 71.5 g of water. To three significant figures (8.0 has two, so the answer is limited to two): 72 g.

Conclusion: 8.0 g of hydrogen makes about 72 g of water — nearly nine times the mass, because the oxygen (from the air) contributes most of the weight. Conservation of mass holds: 8.0 g H2 + 64 g O2 ≈ 72 g H2O.

practice.q: How many moles of oxygen are needed to burn 3.0 mol of propane, C3H8? (C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O)
practice.a: The ratio O2 : C3H8 is 5 : 1, so 3.0 mol × 5 = 15 mol O2.

practice.q: A reaction produces 0.25 mol of CO2. What volume does that occupy at STP?
practice.a: 0.25 mol × 22.4 L/mol = 5.6 L at STP.

lessons.takeaway: Stoichiometry follows one road: grams → moles → mole ratio → moles → grams. The balanced equation supplies the ratio, the molar mass supplies the conversions, and the units check the route.

lessons.title: Limiting Reactants and Percent Yield
lessons.intro: Recipes assume you have every ingredient. Real reactions rarely do. The limiting reactant is the ingredient that runs out first, and it decides how much product can form — no matter how much of everything else you have. And even then, real reactions rarely give the perfect theoretical yield: side reactions, incomplete reactions, and losses in handling all take their cut. Percent yield measures how close reality came to theory.
concepts: The limiting reactant — the reactant that is used up first and limits the amount of product. Find it by converting each reactant to moles of product; the smaller product amount wins, and its reactant is limiting.
The excess reactant — the reactant left over after the limiting one is gone. Excess does not mean unlimited — it is simply the one that survives, partly unconsumed.
Theoretical yield — the maximum product possible if the limiting reactant reacted completely, calculated from stoichiometry. It is the 100% mark.

Actual yield and percent yield — the product actually recovered in the lab. Percent yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100%. Yields above 100% mean the product is wet, impure, or misweighed — never real extra product.

Why yields fall short — reactions that do not go to completion, competing side reactions, and product lost in transfers, filtration, and purification. Industrial chemists spend careers pushing yields up by a few percent.

example.q: A cook has 10 slices of bread and 6 slices of cheese. Each sandwich needs 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. How many sandwiches can be made, what is limiting, and what is left over? Then apply the same logic: 4.0 mol H2 and 1.5 mol O2 react (2H2 + O2 → 2H2O). How much water forms?
steps: First, the sandwiches: bread allows 10 ÷ 2 = 5 sandwiches; cheese allows 6 ÷ 1 = 6. Bread runs out first — bread is limiting, 5 sandwiches form, and 1 slice of cheese is left over.
Second, the chemistry: hydrogen allows 4.0 mol H2 × (2 mol H2O / 2 mol H2) = 4.0 mol H2O. Oxygen allows 1.5 mol O2 × (2 mol H2O / 1 mol O2) = 3.0 mol H2O.
Third, compare: oxygen gives the smaller product amount, so O2 is limiting. Only 3.0 mol of water can form.

Conclusion: 3.0 mol H2O forms, using 3.0 mol H2 — leaving 1.0 mol H2 unreacted as excess. The method is identical to the sandwiches: convert each starting amount to the same product and take the smaller.

practice.q: A student reacts 10.0 g of CaCO3 with excess HCl and recovers 3.50 g of CO2. The theoretical yield is 4.40 g. What is the percent yield?
practice.a: Percent yield = (3.50 ÷ 4.40) × 100% = 79.5%. The missing 20.5% was lost to incomplete reaction and handling.

practice.q: In the reaction N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, you have 1.0 mol N2 and 2.0 mol H2. Which is limiting?
practice.a: N2 allows 1.0 × 2 = 2.0 mol NH3. H2 allows 2.0 × (2/3) = 1.33 mol NH3. Hydrogen gives less, so H2 is limiting, even though there are more moles of it — the ratio, not the raw amount, decides.

lessons.takeaway: The limiting reactant is found by converting every reactant to the same product and taking the smallest result; theoretical yield is the perfect outcome, and percent yield measures how much of it the real world delivered.

lessons.title: Energy Changes in Reactions
lessons.intro: Every chemical reaction trades energy. Break bonds and you must pay energy in; form bonds and energy is paid back out. When the new bonds are stronger than the old ones, the reaction releases heat — exothermic, like a fire. When they are weaker, the reaction absorbs heat — endothermic, like a cold pack. Energy is the other half of every reaction equation, and it decides which reactions can run on their own.
concepts: Exothermic vs endothermic — exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings (temperature rises, ΔH negative): combustion, rusting, neutralization. Endothermic reactions absorb energy (temperature falls, ΔH positive): photosynthesis, melting ice, a cold pack dissolving ammonium nitrate.
Enthalpy (ΔH) — the heat change of a reaction at constant pressure, in kJ per mole of reaction as written. ΔH = energy of bonds broken − energy of bonds formed.

Bond energies — the energy needed to break one mole of a bond in the gas phase. Strong bonds (triple bonds, H–F) have high bond energies; weak bonds break easily. Reaction ΔH can be estimated by adding up the bonds broken and subtracting the bonds formed.

Activation energy — the energy hump a reaction must climb before it can proceed, even an exothermic one. A match provides the activation energy; the fire's own heat then sustains it. Catalysts lower the hump without being consumed.
Energy diagrams — a reaction profile plots energy against progress: reactants, a peak (transition state, height = activation energy), products. Exothermic profiles end lower; endothermic end higher.

example.q: Use bond energies to estimate ΔH for H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–H 436 kJ/mol, Cl–Cl 242 kJ/mol, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol.
steps: First, bonds broken: one H–H bond (436) + one Cl–Cl bond (242) = 678 kJ/mol put in.
Second, bonds formed: two H–Cl bonds = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ/mol paid back out.
Third, ΔH = energy in − energy out = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol. Negative means energy released: the reaction is exothermic.

Conclusion: the new H–Cl bonds are stronger than the old H–H and Cl–Cl bonds, so the reaction pays out more energy than it costs — which is why hydrogen and chlorine react with a flash of light and heat. (The experimental value is −185 kJ/mol: the estimate is remarkably close.)

practice.q: A reaction has ΔH = +57 kJ/mol. Is it exothermic or endothermic, and does the temperature of the surroundings rise or fall?
practice.a: Endothermic — positive ΔH means heat is absorbed from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool down (which is how instant cold packs work).

practice.q: Why does a catalyst speed up a reaction without changing its ΔH?
practice.a: A catalyst provides a different pathway with a lower activation energy, so more molecules can clear the hump — but it changes neither the reactants' nor the products' energies, so ΔH, the difference between them, is unchanged.

lessons.takeaway: Breaking bonds costs energy, forming bonds releases it; if the products' bonds are stronger, the reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative), and activation energy is the hump every reaction must climb first — a hump catalysts lower.

lessons.title: Gases and the Gas Laws
lessons.intro: Gases are the most predictable state of matter, because gas particles are so far apart that they barely notice each other. Four variables describe a gas — pressure, volume, temperature, and amount — and the gas laws tie them together so tightly that knowing any three tells you the fourth. From a balloon rising to a scuba tank, the same few equations run the show.
concepts: Pressure — force per unit area, from gas particles colliding with walls. Units: atmospheres (atm), mmHg (torr), pascals (Pa). 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.3 kPa. Pressure rises when particles hit harder or more often.
Boyle's law — at constant temperature and amount, pressure and volume are inversely related: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. Squeeze a gas into half the volume and its pressure doubles.
Charles's law — at constant pressure and amount, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. Temperature must be in kelvin, never Celsius. Heat a gas and it expands.

Avogadro's law and the combined gas law — equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of particles. The combined law, P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, handles changes in all three variables at once.

The ideal gas law — PV = nRT, where R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). It links all four variables and lets you find moles from a gas's pressure, volume, and temperature — or find density and molar mass from gas measurements.

example.q: A balloon holds 2.00 L of helium at 1.00 atm and 25 °C (298 K). It rises to an altitude where the pressure is 0.50 atm and the temperature is −23 °C (250 K). What is the balloon's new volume?
steps: First, choose the combined gas law, since P, V, and T all change while the amount stays fixed: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
Second, convert temperatures to kelvin (already done: 298 K and 250 K) and rearrange: V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 2.00 L × (1.00/0.50) × (250/298).
Third, calculate: (1.00/0.50) = 2.00 doubles the volume (pressure halved); (250/298) = 0.839 shrinks it slightly (colder). V₂ = 2.00 × 2.00 × 0.839 = 3.36 L.
Conclusion: the balloon expands to 3.36 L — the pressure drop dominates the cooling. If the temperature had been left in Celsius, the ratio would have been nonsense: kelvin is mandatory in gas laws.

practice.q: A gas at 2.0 atm occupies 4.0 L at constant temperature. It is compressed to 1.0 L. What is its new pressure?
practice.a: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → P₂ = (2.0 × 4.0) / 1.0 = 8.0 atm. Quartering the volume quadruples the pressure.

practice.q: How many moles of gas are in a 10.0 L tank at 2.00 atm and 300 K? (R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K))

lessons.takeaway: Four variables describe a gas, and the gas laws connect them: Boyle ties pressure to volume, Charles ties volume to kelvin temperature, and PV = nRT ties all four together — with temperature always in kelvin.

lessons.title: Liquids, Solids and Intermolecular Forces
lessons.intro: Why is water a liquid at room temperature while carbon dioxide is a gas, and why does a diamond never melt in a kitchen oven? The answer is not in the molecules themselves but in the forces between them — intermolecular forces. They are weaker than chemical bonds, but they decide whether a substance is a solid, liquid, or gas, how high it boils, and whether it dissolves. The strongest forces make the highest boiling points.
concepts: Kinetic molecular theory — particles are always moving; temperature measures their average kinetic energy. In solids they vibrate in place, in liquids they slide past each other, in gases they fly freely.

London dispersion forces — present in ALL molecules: momentary uneven electron clouds create temporary dipoles that attract neighbours. They grow with size and surface area — big molecules have stronger dispersion forces and higher boiling points.

Dipole–dipole forces — between polar molecules, the positive end of one attracts the negative end of another. Stronger than dispersion forces between similar-sized molecules, which is why polar substances usually boil higher than nonpolar ones of the same size.

Hydrogen bonding — the strongest intermolecular force: a hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F is strongly attracted to a lone pair on N, O, or F of another molecule. It is why water boils at 100 °C while similar-sized H2S boils at −60 °C.

Solids: crystalline vs amorphous — crystalline solids (salt, diamond, ice) have ordered lattices and sharp melting points; amorphous solids (glass, plastic) have disordered structures and soften gradually. Network covalent solids like diamond are held by bonds, not intermolecular forces, so their melting points are enormous.

example.q: Rank these by boiling point, lowest to highest, and explain: CH4 (methane), H2O (water), NaCl (sodium chloride).
steps: First, methane: a small nonpolar molecule held together only by weak London dispersion forces. It boils at −161 °C — the lowest by far.
Second, water: small too, but its molecules hydrogen-bond to each other — the strongest intermolecular force. It boils at 100 °C, remarkably high for so small a molecule.
Third, sodium chloride: not molecules at all, but a lattice of ions held by ionic bonds — forces far stronger than any intermolecular force. It melts at 801 °C and boils at 1413 °C.

Conclusion: boiling point ranks with the strength of what must be broken — dispersion forces, then hydrogen bonds, then full ionic bonds. Water's famous high boiling point is a hydrogen-bonding effect.

practice.q: Why does ethanol (CH3CH2OH) dissolve in water but hexane (C6H14) does not?
practice.a: Ethanol's –OH group hydrogen-bonds with water, so mixing costs little energy; hexane is nonpolar and can only offer weak dispersion forces, so water molecules would rather stay bonded to each other than make room for it — like dissolves like.

practice.q: Why does ice float on water, and what does that have to do with hydrogen bonding?
practice.a: In ice, hydrogen bonds lock water molecules into an open, spacious lattice with empty space — so ice is less dense than liquid water, where molecules pack more closely. That floating ice insulates lakes in winter, protecting life below.

lessons.takeaway: Intermolecular forces rank: dispersion (all molecules) < dipole–dipole (polar molecules) < hydrogen bonding (H on N, O, or F) < ionic bonds (lattices) — and that ladder explains boiling points, solubility, and why ice floats.

lessons.title: Solutions and Concentration (Molarity)
lessons.intro: Most chemistry happens in solution — a uniform mixture where one substance (the solute) is dissolved in another (the solvent). The sea, your blood, and the coffee on your desk are all solutions. Concentration says how much solute is in a given amount of solution, and molarity — moles per litre — is the unit chemists use most, because it plugs straight into stoichiometry. Dilution is just spreading the same moles over more litres.
concepts: Molarity — M = moles of solute ÷ litres of solution. A 1.0 M solution holds 1.0 mole per litre. Molarity is temperature-dependent (volumes change with temperature), but for lab work it is the standard.

Preparing a solution — moles needed = molarity × volume (in litres); weigh that many grams of solute, dissolve, then add solvent up to the final volume — not the other way around. Volume is measured after mixing.

Dilution — adding solvent does not change the moles of solute: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. To make a dilute solution from a concentrated stock, calculate the stock volume needed, then add solvent to the final volume.

Solubility — the maximum solute that dissolves at a given temperature. Some salts dissolve readily (NaCl); others barely (AgCl). Temperature usually raises the solubility of solids but lowers that of gases — warm soda goes flat.

Electrolytes — solutes that produce ions in water and conduct electricity: strong electrolytes (soluble salts, strong acids) dissociate completely; weak electrolytes (acetic acid) partly; nonelectrolytes (sugar, ethanol) do not dissociate at all.

example.q: How many grams of NaCl are needed to make 500 mL of 0.250 M solution? And how would you dilute 50.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl to 0.500 M?
steps: First, moles of NaCl: 0.500 L × 0.250 mol/L = 0.125 mol. (500 mL must be converted to 0.500 L first — molarity is per litre.)
Second, grams: molar mass of NaCl is 58.44 g/mol, so 0.125 mol × 58.44 g/mol = 7.31 g. Weigh 7.31 g, dissolve in some water, then add water until the total volume is exactly 500 mL.
Third, the dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ → V₂ = (2.00 M × 50.0 mL) / 0.500 M = 200 mL. The final volume is 200 mL, so add 150 mL of water to the 50.0 mL of stock.
Conclusion: the moles of solute never change in a dilution — only the volume does. Check: 2.00 M × 50 mL = 100 mmol; 0.500 M × 200 mL = 100 mmol. The moles match.

practice.q: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 4.00 g of NaOH (molar mass 40.00 g/mol) in enough water to make 250 mL?
A sports drink label says it contains 0.020 M Na+. How many moles of Na+ are in a 500 mL bottle?

lessons.takeaway: Molarity is moles per litre of solution; to make a solution, weigh the moles and fill to the final volume, and to dilute, use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ — the moles of solute stay the same while the volume grows.

lessons.title: Acids and Bases: A First Look
lessons.intro: Vinegar stings, soap feels slippery, and your stomach runs on acid strong enough to dissolve metal — yet your blood stays almost perfectly neutral. Acids and bases are the great opposites of chemistry, and their reactions are everywhere: digestion, cleaning, ocean chemistry, and the soil. The definitions are simple — acids donate protons, bases accept them — and the pH scale turns that into a single number.
concepts: Arrhenius and Brønsted–Lowry definitions — an Arrhenius acid releases H+ in water; a Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton (H+) to another substance, and a base accepts it. Every Arrhenius acid is a Brønsted acid; the Brønsted definition also works outside water.

Strong vs weak — a strong acid (HCl, HNO3, H2SO4) dissociates completely in water; a weak acid (acetic acid, CH3COOH) dissociates only partly, reaching equilibrium. Strong refers to completeness of dissociation, not to danger or concentration.
The pH scale — pH = −log[H+]. Pure water has [H+] = 10^-7 M, so pH 7 is neutral; below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic. Each whole pH unit is a tenfold change: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.
Neutralization — acid + base → salt + water. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O. The net ionic equation is the heart of it: H+ + OH- → H2O.

Indicators and the pH of everyday things — litmus turns red in acid and blue in base; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base. Lemon juice is ~pH 2, blood ~7.4, oven cleaner ~13. Buffers resist pH change — blood is buffered, which is why it stays at 7.4.

example.q: A sample of rainwater has [H+] = 1.0 × 10^-5 M. What is its pH, and is it acidic, neutral, or basic? If a lake's pH falls from 6.0 to 5.0, how much more acidic has it become?
steps: First, pH = −log(1.0 × 10^-5) = 5.0. Since 5.0 is below 7, the rainwater is acidic — normal rain is slightly acidic (pH ~5.6) from dissolved CO2, and this sample is a little more acidic still.
Second, the lake: pH is logarithmic, so a drop of one unit means [H+] multiplied by 10. Falling from 6.0 to 5.0 means the water is ten times more acidic.
Third, connect to chemistry: more H+ means less carbonate available for shell-building animals and more toxic aluminium leaching from soils — small pH numbers hide large chemical changes.
Conclusion: pH turns a concentration into a readable number, and because the scale is logarithmic, one unit is a factor of ten, not a small step.

practice.q: Write the neutralization equation for sulfuric acid with potassium hydroxide, and identify the salt.
practice.a: H2SO4 + 2KOH → K2SO4 + 2H2O. The salt is potassium sulfate, K2SO4.

practice.q: Is a 0.10 M solution of acetic acid (a weak acid) more or less acidic than a 0.10 M solution of HCl (a strong acid)? Why?
practice.a: Less acidic. HCl dissociates completely, so [H+] ≈ 0.10 M (pH 1); acetic acid dissociates only a few percent, so [H+] is far lower (pH ~2.9). Same concentration, different strength.

lessons.takeaway: Acids donate protons, bases accept them; strong means fully dissociated, not concentrated; pH = −log[H+] with 7 neutral and each unit a tenfold change; and acid plus base makes salt plus water.

lessons.title: Final Review and Problem-Solving Lab
lessons.intro: This is the capstone of General Chemistry I — not a new topic, but a workout that ties the whole course together. Real chemistry problems are rarely one-step: a question may ask you to balance an equation, find the limiting reactant, compute a percent yield, and check the answer against conservation of mass, all in one chain. The method is always the same: write down what you know, convert to moles, follow the ratios, and check the units and the size of the answer.
concepts: The master roadmap — grams ⇄ moles ⇄ particles ⇄ litres of gas, all connected through molar mass, Avogadro's number, and 22.4 L/mol at STP, with the balanced equation's mole ratios at the centre. Every stoichiometry problem is a walk on this map.
Significant figures in chains — carry extra digits through intermediate steps and round only at the end; the final answer is limited by the least precise measurement in the chain.
Naming and formulas as a check — before calculating, write the correct formulas: ionic compounds balance charges, covalent compounds count atoms. A wrong formula makes every later step wrong.
Energy and states as context — is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? Is the product a gas (volume matters) or a precipitate (it leaves the solution)? The physical picture guides the calculation.

Lab safety as chemistry — every calculation in this course exists to keep a real lab safe: the right mass, the right concentration, the limiting reactant known in advance. A molarity error is not just a lost mark — it is a wrong solution in a real flask.

example.q: A student reacts 25.0 g of zinc with excess hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. What volume of hydrogen gas is produced at STP, and how many grams of ZnCl2 form?
steps: First, moles of zinc: molar mass Zn = 65.38 g/mol, so 25.0 g ÷ 65.38 g/mol = 0.382 mol Zn.
Second, hydrogen: the ratio Zn : H2 is 1:1, so 0.382 mol H2 forms. At STP, 0.382 mol × 22.4 L/mol = 8.56 L of hydrogen gas.
Third, zinc chloride: the ratio Zn : ZnCl2 is also 1:1, so 0.382 mol ZnCl2 forms. Its molar mass is 65.38 + 2(35.45) = 136.28 g/mol, so mass = 0.382 × 136.28 = 52.1 g.

Conclusion: 25.0 g of zinc gives 8.56 L of H2 and 52.1 g of ZnCl2. Check by mass: reactants 25.0 g Zn + 27.8 g HCl = 52.8 g; products 52.1 g ZnCl2 + 0.77 g H2 = 52.9 g (rounding) — conservation of mass holds, and the answer is consistent.

practice.q: Balance and solve: 12.0 g of Mg reacts with excess O2 (2Mg + O2 → 2MgO). What mass of MgO forms?
practice.a: Moles Mg = 12.0 ÷ 24.31 = 0.494 mol; ratio Mg : MgO is 1:1, so 0.494 mol MgO; molar mass MgO = 40.31 g/mol; mass = 0.494 × 40.31 = 19.9 g.

practice.q: A 0.500 M NaOH solution neutralizes 25.0 mL of 0.200 M HCl. What volume of NaOH is needed? (HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O)
practice.a: Moles HCl = 0.0250 L × 0.200 mol/L = 0.00500 mol; ratio 1:1, so 0.00500 mol NaOH needed; volume = 0.00500 ÷ 0.500 = 0.0100 L = 10.0 mL.

lessons.takeaway: Every problem in this course is one roadmap: formulas right, equation balanced, grams to moles, mole ratio, moles to the wanted unit — then check the answer by size, units, and conservation of mass.
